# Rasterization Variant


## Overview
This family defines the specific algorithmic variations of the differentiable rasterization pipeline used to render 3D Gaussians, extending the standard alpha-compositing logic of [3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer](2813-3d-gaussian-splatting-differentiable-rasterizer.md). It addresses specialized requirements such as dynamic pruning gradients, X-ray physics, hybrid sigma fallbacks, and importance scoring, which the base rasterizer does not natively support.

## Shared principles
All variants in this family operate on the same fundamental data structures: a set of 3D Gaussians defined by mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, opacity $\alpha$, and color/features. They share the initial projection step, transforming 3D parameters to 2D screen space using extrinsic/intrinsic matrices and Jacobian transformations to compute 2D covariances. They all utilize a tile-based sorting and accumulation strategy to ensure depth ordering and correct alpha blending. The core divergence lies in how the alpha value $\alpha_i$ is computed, how the blending loop modifies the transmittance $T$ and color $C$, and what auxiliary data (masks, counts, or physics parameters) is propagated.

## Subtopics

### [Masked-Rasterization](4366-masked-rasterization.md)
Masked-rasterization allows "masked" (probabilistically unused) 3D Gaussians to participate in the rasterization pipeline and receive gradient updates, rather than being strictly culled. It solves the problem of gradient starvation in dynamic pruning scenarios, where Gaussians with zero opacity or scale are filtered out before rasterization and thus cannot update their existence probability. Unlike standard rasterization variants that treat Gaussians as binary present/absent entities based on static attributes, this method applies masks during the blending process to enable dynamic assessment of a Gaussian's contribution.

### [Differentiable Radiative Rasterization](4526-differentiable-radiative-rasterization.md)
Differentiable Radiative Rasterization (DRR) is a GPU-accelerated rasterization method designed to render novel X-ray projections from radiative 3D Gaussian point clouds. It solves the problem of differentiable volume rendering for X-ray imaging, where the "volume" is represented by a set of Gaussians with associated radiation intensities rather than standard RGB colors. DRR distinguishes itself from sibling methods like [3D/2D Hybrid Gaussian Rasterization with Fallback Sigma](4812-3d-2d-hybrid-gaussian-rasterization-with-fallback-sigma.md) by specifically modeling the physics of X-ray attenuation and source-detector geometry, using a specific Jacobian for the X-ray projection and a radiative intensity accumulation model.

### [3D/2D Hybrid Gaussian Rasterization with Fallback Sigma](4812-3d-2d-hybrid-gaussian-rasterization-with-fallback-sigma.md)
This method renders 3D Gaussians by combining a screen-space 2D Gaussian approximation with a ray-surfel 3D sigma calculation to determine the tighter bounding sigma for alpha attenuation. It computes a fallback 2D sigma based on pre-computed screen-space means and selects the minimum of the 3D and 2D sigmas to define the effective spread for each Gaussian during accumulation.

### [Gaussian Rasterization with F-Count](17250-gaussian-rasterization-with-f-count.md)
This variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting extends the standard differentiable rasterizer to output the number of times each Gaussian is activated (rendered) during the forward pass, alongside the standard color and radii tensors. It is primarily used in LightGaussian to compute importance scores for Gaussian pruning and compression. It differs from the standard rasterizer by invoking a specialized C++/CUDA kernel (`count_gaussians`) that tracks per-Gaussian activation counts, whereas siblings like Masked-Rasterization focus on visibility masking or Differentiable Radiative Rasterization focuses on radiative transfer physics.

### Analytic Tau Rasterization
- **Definition**: A rasterization branch (`use_analytic_tau`) that computes the per-pixel accumulated analytic line-integral optical thickness $\tau$ along the view ray. Alpha is derived physically as $\text{alpha} = 1 - \text{exp}(-\tau)$ using Beer-Lambert extinction, rather than using heuristic alpha values [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The base differentiable rasterizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The variants described here emerge from subsequent research into optimizing training dynamics (Masked-Rasterization, F-Count), extending the representation to non-visible spectra (DRR), and improving numerical stability or approximation accuracy (Hybrid Sigma, Analytic Tau). The codebase structure, particularly the CUDA extensions in `diff-gaussian-rasterization`, supports these variants through conditional compilation or runtime flags, as seen in the `4DGS-Volume-Cloud` repository which integrates analytic-tau and other channels [S1, unofficial].
